description_en: The label "First Roman Emperor" is a modern historiographical category, not an ancient title. Augustus held no constitutional office called emperor. He was princeps (first citizen), and his power derived from a bundle of specific powers.

Augustus claimed to have restored the Republic in the Res Gestae. Modern scholarship views the 27 BCE settlement as a carefully managed political performance that established de facto autocracy under republican forms.
Rumors that Livia poisoned Augustus appear in Tacitus (Annals 1.5-6) and Cassius Dio. Most modern historians reject this as hostile tradition rather than historical fact.

The "First Triumvirate" label (Caesar, Pompey, Crassus) was coined by modern historians by analogy with the Second Triumvirate. Neither was formally called a triumvirate in its own time, though the Second was legally constituted by the Lex Titia.

Augustus official portraits were idealized and deliberately ageless—he is depicted as perpetually youthful from 29 BCE until his death at 75, a calculated departure from realistic late-Republican veristic portraiture.
